chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from a man who named him, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim al-Ja'fari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The world yearned for a people with purely permissible earnings, but they did not desire it, so they passed by. Then it yearned for a people with permissible and doubtful earnings, so they said, 'We have no need for the doubtful,' and they expanded within the permissible. Then it yearned for another people with prohibited and doubtful earnings, so they said, 'We have no need for the prohibited,' and they expanded within the doubtful. Then it yearned for a people with purely prohibited earnings, so they sought it, but they could not find it. And the believer in the world eats at the status of the desperate (one who eats only out of necessity).

key_terms.بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْمُضْطَرِّ: At the status of the desperate/necessity-driven

ai.seo_question: How does a believer approach worldly earnings according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi outlines a descending hierarchy of worldly attachment, where individuals progressively compromise their spiritual integrity by accepting doubtful (shubha) and then purely prohibited (haram) earnings. In Shia jurisprudence, this serves as a foundational principle for 'ihtiyat' (precaution), urging believers to treat permissible sustenance with the humility of the 'muqtarid' (one in dire need) to avoid the subtle corruption of doubt. It highlights that true piety is not merely avoiding the blatantly haram, but actively shunning the ambiguous to preserve the purity of the soul.
